Q: Azure redis cluster key event invalidation events A:

Keyspace notifications aren't reliable for this across a cluster -- you can miss events, and as you've found there's an open PR for proper cluster notification support that never landed.

Redis 6+ has a purpose-built mechanism for this: CLIENT TRACKING. Instead of subscribing to keyspace events, your connection tells Redis which keys it's tracking and the server pushes an invalidation directly when one changes, regardless of which instance wrote it. No missed events, and it still respects TTLs.

StackExchange.Redis doesn't implement CLIENT TRACKING itself, so I built RedisNearCache (https://github.com/magna-nz/redis-near-cache) as a layer on top of it that handles the tracking/invalidation and keeps a local copy in sync.

Disclosure: I'm the author.

Q: How Microsoft HybridCache works in a Microservice Setup with Multiple Pods A:

HybridCache doesn't have anything built in for this today — RemoveAsync clears both local and distributed cache, and there's no way to only invalidate the local copy in other pods from one place.

If you want actual cross-pod invalidation rather than working around it with your own pub/sub, Redis 6+ has CLIENT TRACKING: the server tracks what each connection has read and pushes an invalidation the moment any of it changes, from any pod.

I built RedisNearCache (https://github.com/magna-nz/redis-near-cache) on top of StackExchange.Redis to do exactly this — it has a HybridCache adapter (AddRedisNearCacheHybridCache()) that replaces HybridCache's own L1 with one that gets evicted correctly across pods instead of just on a TTL.

Disclosure: I'm the author.

Q: Do concurrent accesses to a volatile glvalue result in undefined behavior or implementation-defined behavior? A:

From your comment:

I think you misunderstand my question. I didn't ask whether the implementation is permitted to provide guaranteed behavior for undefined operations. Since the semantics of the access are implementation-defined, and the instance of the abstract machine is parameterized by the implementation-defined behavior, the implementation can specify the semantics as they were atomic operations, which wouldn't violate the data-race rule, so that the program doesn't have data-race UB; this is the question I asked.

You need to understand the distinction between the standard behavior and the "compiler behavior".

A compiler can implement it's behavior however it wants. Really. If the behavior the compiler implements doesn't fall within the behavior described by the standard, then that compiler implementation is not standard. To be clear I don't mean locking down a specific behavior in the case of the standard UB or implementation defined behavior. I mean not following the behavior described by the standard. And this is not just a hypothetical, all compiler do this (either by flags, or even by default).

From the standard point of view, the program you've showed is Undefined Behavior. It says so point blank.

A compiler may choose to define the behavior of that code as well behaved and deterministic.

Now, you may still insist upon questioning if, from the standard behavior, if an implementation defined behavior defined that volatile is atomic, then does that mean that it is NOT Undefined Behavior from the point of the standard? Honestly I ... don't know. I think that is not a valid conclusion. But, and there is a big but. This question has no real value. Whatever the answer is, it doesn't matter in any way, shape or form. You can't rely on that code to be portable. You would have to rely on the behavior of the specific compiler. If that behavior falls within the standard implementation defined behavior, undefined behavior, or is just not standard behavior, it doesn't matter. It's still the specific behavior of the compiler you need to rely on.

Q: Concordance correlation coefficient for negative correaltion A:

from this blog-post:
https://python-bloggers.com/2024/10/step-by-step-guide-to-using-the-concordance-correlation-coefficient/

  • A CCC value close to -1 suggests high negative agreement, indicating a strong linear relationship, but one dataset is the mirror image of the other.

ie ccc = -1.0 if x[0] == y[-1], x[1] == y[-2] ....
if you run ccc(x, 1-y) then you indeed get -1.0 correlation, thus there is nothing wrong with your formula (also the log reports the formula to be the one you used)

Q: Excel Sum Index Match Across Multiple columns A:
